metadata.title: On the Capacity of the 2-user Gaussian MAC Interfering with a P2P Link

extraction_notes.note: The proof-sketch rule asks for rigor semi_formal on a sketch proof, while the rigor rule forbids rigor on proofs; followed the sketch rule (alternative proves edge) but the finishing step rejects rigor on a proof, so the sketches carry no rigor field, the appendix proofs carry the full argument.
Parameter-regime conditions ('Consider a PIMAC ... such that', 'Suppose that the PIMAC has') could be definitions of interference regimes; typed assumption since they are hypotheses of Theorems 3-5.
The paper writes the MAC region both as \mathcal{C}^M and \mathcal{C}_M for the same object; treated as one definition.
Theorems 3-5 are argued in running text before their environments; the argument spans were taken from the first sentence after the regime conditions to 'we have/obtain the following theorem'.

nodes.name: Multiple access channel (MAC)
nodes.statement: The multiple access channel (MAC) is a scenario where several transmitters want to deliver one message each to one receiver.
differentia: several transmitters want to deliver one message each to one receiver

nodes.name: Interference channel (IC)
nodes.statement: The interference channel (IC) is another well studied model in information theory, that is a model where two transmit-receive pairs want to communicate while causing interference to each other.
differentia: two transmit-receive pairs want to communicate while causing interference to each other

nodes.name: PIMAC (P2P channel interfering with a 2-user MAC)
differentia: A Gaussian 2-user multiple access channel (MAC) and a Gaussian point-to-point (P2P) channel use the same medium for their communication
also_stated_at: The obtained setup consists of a point-to-point (P2P) channel interfering with with a 2-user MAC and we call it a (PIMAC).
nodes.statement_short: Gaussian 2-user MAC and a P2P channel sharing a medium; outputs $Y_1,Y_2$ with cross gains $h_{ij}$ and unit-variance AWGN.

nodes.name: Power constraint
nodes.statement: Transmitter $i$ has power constraint $P_i$ so that $\mathbb{E}[X_i^2]\leq P_i$.

nodes.name: Messages and codewords
nodes.statement: The transmitters encode their messages $m_i$ chosen independently from $\mathcal{M}_i=\{1,\dots,2^{nR_i}\}$ into a codeword  of length $n$ symbols $X_i^n\in\mathbb{R}^n$ $$X_i^n=(X_{i,1},\dots,X_{i,n})$$ using encoding functions $f_i$.
nodes.statement_short: Each transmitter encodes a message $m_i\in\mathcal{M}_i$ into a length-$n$ codeword $X_i^n$.

nodes.name: Decoding error
nodes.statement: A decoding error $E_i$ occurs if $m_i\neq\hat{m}_i$.

nodes.name: Code and average error probability
nodes.statement_short: A code is encoders, decoders and message sets; its average error probability $P^{(n)}$ averages the union error over messages.

nodes.name: Achievable rate tuple
nodes.statement: A rate tuple $(R_1,R_2,R_3)$ is achievable if there exists a sequence of $(n,2^{nR_1},2^{nR_2},2^{nR_3})$ codes such that $P^{(n)}]\to0$ as $n\to\infty$.
differentia: there exists a sequence of $(n,2^{nR_1},2^{nR_2},2^{nR_3})$ codes such that $P^{(n)}]\to0$ as $n\to\infty$

nodes.name: Capacity region and sum capacity
MAC capacity region $\mathcal{C}^M(\mathcal{S},j)$
nodes.statement_short: $M(\mathcal{S},j)$ is the Gaussian MAC from transmitters in $\mathcal{S}$ to receiver $j$; its capacity region is the usual polymatroid of sum-rate bounds.

nodes.name: Outer bound on the PIMAC capacity region
conclusions: The capacity region of the PIMAC is outer bounded by $\overline{\mathcal{C}}$
nodes.statement_short: $\mathcal{C}\subseteq\overline{\mathcal{C}}$: P2P and MAC bounds plus Sato-type MAC bounds at each receiver whenever the relevant cross gain is at least 1.
nodes.label: pSILemma

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 1 (pointer)
nodes.statement: The proof is based on arguments similar to Sato's arguments in \cite{Sato} and is given in Appendix \ref{pSILemmaProof}.
nodes.statement_short: Sato-type argument; deferred to the appendix.

nodes.name: Inner bound on the PIMAC capacity region
conclusions: The capacity region of the PIMAC is inner bounded by $\underline{\mathcal{C}}$
nodes.statement_short: Rates in both 3-user MAC regions (to receiver 1 and to receiver 2) are achievable.
nodes.label: InnerBound

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 1
nodes.statement: Each receiver simply decodes all messages in a MAC fashion. The achievable rates must be in the intersection of $\mathcal{C}_M(\{1,2,3\},1)$ and $\mathcal{C}_M(\{1,2,3\},2)$ and the statement of the theorem follows.
nodes.statement_short: Each receiver decodes all messages as in a MAC, giving the intersection of the two MAC regions.

nodes.name: Capacity region of the PIMAC with strong interference
conclusions: the outer bound $\overline{\mathcal{C}}$ and the inner bound $\underline{\mathcal{C}}$ coincide
nodes.statement_short: Under strong interference and a power condition, the outer and inner bounds coincide and give the capacity region.
nodes.label: pSITheorem

nodes.name: Proof sketch of Theorem 2
nodes.statement: By expanding the achievable region $\underline{\mathcal{C}}$, and using conditions (\ref{pSI1}) and (\ref{pSI2}), it can be shown that $\underline{\mathcal{C}}$ reduces to $\overline{\mathcal{C}}$ and the result follows. Details are given in Appendix \ref{pSIProof}.
nodes.statement_short: Expand the inner bound and use the two conditions to reduce it to the outer bound; details in the appendix.

nodes.name: Strong-interference capacity as intersection of two MAC regions
nodes.statement: In conclusion, if the PIMAC has strong interference, i.e. (\ref{pSI1}) is satisfied, and if (\ref{pSI2}) holds, then the capacity region of the PIMAC is the intersection of two MAC capacity regions, from all transmitters to each receiver.

nodes.name: PIMAC with strong interference
nodes.statement: Let us now consider special cases of the PIMAC with strong interference $h_{12}^2,h_{22}^2,h_{31}^2\geq1$.

nodes.name: Outer bound under strong interference
nodes.statement:
According to Lemma \ref{pSILemma}, any achievable rate tuple $(R_1,R_2,R_3)\in\mathbb{R}_+^3$ for PIMAC with strong interference must satisfy
\begin{align} (R_1,R_3)&\in\mathcal{C}_M(\{1,3\},2)\\ (R_2,R_3)&\in\mathcal{C}_M(\{2,3\},2)\\ (R_1,R_2,R_3)&\in\mathcal{C}_M(\{1,2,3\},1).
\end{align}
where the remaining bounds $R_3\leq\frac{1}{2}\log(1+P_3)$ and $(R_1,R_2)\in\mathcal{C}^M(\{1,2\},1)$ were removed because they are already included in (\ref{SIB3})-(\ref{SIB5}).
assumptions: any achievable rate tuple $(R_1,R_2,R_3)\in\mathbb{R}_+^3$ for PIMAC with strong interference
nodes.statement_short: Under strong interference Lemma 1 reduces to three MAC constraints; the P2P and receiver-1 MAC bounds are implied.

nodes.name: Very strong interference from transmitter 1 to receiver 2
nodes.statement:
Consider a PIMAC with strong interference such that interference from transmitter 1 to receiver 2 is very strong, 
\begin{align} h_{12}^2&\geq1+P_3+h_{22}^2P_2\\
h_{22}^2&\geq1\\ h_{31}^2&\geq1.
\end{align}
nodes.section: 4.1 Very strong interference from transmitter 1 to receiver 2

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 3
nodes.section: 4.1 Very strong interference from transmitter 1 to receiver 2
nodes.statement_short: Show bound (9) is redundant, then achieve the reduced outer bound: receiver 2 decodes $X_1$ first treating others as noise, then a MAC; receiver 1 decodes all.

nodes.name: Reduce the outer bound
nodes.section: 4.1 Very strong interference from transmitter 1 to receiver 2
nodes.statement_short: Bound (9) is redundant, so the outer bound reduces to two MAC constraints.

nodes.name: Receiver 2 decodes $X_1$ first
nodes.section: 4.1 Very strong interference from transmitter 1 to receiver 2
nodes.statement_short: Very strong interference lets receiver 2 decode $X_1^n$ treating the rest as noise at no rate cost.

nodes.name: Achieve the reduced outer bound
nodes.statement: Then by subtracting the contribution of $X_1^n$ from $Y_2^n$, and decoding $X_2^n$ and $X_3^n$ in a MAC fashion at the second receiver, the rate region $\mathcal{C}^M(\{2,3\},2)$ can be achieved. If the first receiver decodes all signals in a MAC fashion, the rate region $\mathcal{C}_M(\{1,2,3\},1)$ can be achieved. Therefore we have the following theorem.
nodes.section: 4.1 Very strong interference from transmitter 1 to receiver 2
nodes.statement_short: Successive decoding at receiver 2 and MAC decoding at receiver 1 achieve the reduced outer bound.

nodes.name: Capacity region under very strong interference from transmitter 1 to receiver 2
nodes.section: 4.1 Very strong interference from transmitter 1 to receiver 2
nodes.statement_short: With very strong interference from transmitter 1 to receiver 2, the capacity region is the intersection of two MAC regions.

nodes.name: Analogous result for transmitter 2 to receiver 2
nodes.statement: Similarly if interference from transmitter 2 to receiver 2 is very strong.
nodes.section: 4.1 Very strong interference from transmitter 1 to receiver 2
nodes.statement_short: The same capacity result holds, by symmetry, when interference from transmitter 2 to receiver 2 is very strong.

nodes.name: Very strong interference from transmitter 3 to receiver 1
nodes.statement:
Suppose that the PIMAC has
\begin{align} h_{12}^2&\geq1\\
h_{22}^2&\geq1\\ h_{31}^2&\geq1+P_1+P_2.
\end{align}

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 4
nodes.section: 4.2 Very strong interference from transmitter 3 to receiver 1
nodes.statement_short: Derive a reduced outer bound, then achieve it: receiver 1 decodes $X_3$ first, receiver 2 decodes all, with (24) making the sum bound redundant.

nodes.name: Reduced outer bound
nodes.section: 4.2 Very strong interference from transmitter 3 to receiver 1
nodes.statement_short: Under (20), bound (11) is replaced by the receiver-1 MAC bound on $(R_1,R_2)$, giving an outer bound.

nodes.name: Receiver 1 decodes $X_3$ first
nodes.section: 4.2 Very strong interference from transmitter 3 to receiver 1
nodes.statement_short: Condition (20) lets receiver 1 decode and cancel $X_3^n$, then achieve $\mathcal{C}^M(\{1,2\},1)$.

nodes.name: Sum bound at receiver 2 is redundant
nodes.section: 4.2 Very strong interference from transmitter 3 to receiver 1
nodes.statement_short: Receiver 2 decodes all; under (24) its 3-user sum-rate bound is redundant, leaving pairwise MAC bounds.

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: Now, since the region $\mathcal{C}_M(\{1,2\},2)$ is larger than $\mathcal{C}_M(\{1,2\},1)$, we obtain the following theorem.
nodes.section: 4.2 Very strong interference from transmitter 3 to receiver 1
nodes.statement_short: The receiver-2 bound on $(R_1,R_2)$ is looser, so the achievable region matches the outer bound.

nodes.name: Capacity region under very strong interference from transmitter 3 to receiver 1
nodes.section: 4.2 Very strong interference from transmitter 3 to receiver 1
nodes.statement_short: Under conditions (18)-(20) and (24), the capacity region is given by three pairwise MAC constraints.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 5
nodes.section: 4.3 The PIMAC with very strong interference
nodes.statement_short: The interference-free bound is an outer bound; decoding interference first at each receiver and cancelling it achieves it.

nodes.name: Interference-free outer bound
nodes.section: 4.3 The PIMAC with very strong interference
nodes.statement_short: The P2P capacity and the interference-free MAC region bound the rates.

nodes.name: Achieve by decoding interference first
nodes.statement: This outer bound can be achieved under the given conditions (\ref{pIMAC-VSI1}) and (\ref{pIMAC-VSI2}) by decoding interference first at each receiver while treating the desired signal as noise, and then decoding the desired signal after removing the contribution of interference. Thus, as if interference is not present, the capacity region of the pIMAC becomes as given in the following theorem.
nodes.section: 4.3 The PIMAC with very strong interference
nodes.statement_short: Each receiver decodes and cancels interference first, achieving the outer bound.

nodes.name: Capacity region of the PIMAC with very strong interference
nodes.section: 4.3 The PIMAC with very strong interference
also_stated_at: In this case, interference does not reduce capacity, i.e. the capacity region of the interference free MAC $M(\{1,2\},1)$ can be achieved by $(R_1,R_2)$ and the point-to-point capacity $R_3=\frac{1}{2}\log(1+P_3)$ can also be achieved.
nodes.statement_short: Under very strong interference the PIMAC achieves the interference-free MAC region and the P2P capacity.

nodes.name: Sum capacity upper bound for the PIMAC
conclusions: The sum capacity of the PIMAC is upper bounded by $\overline{C}_\Sigma$
nodes.statement_short: Genie-aided sum capacity upper bound: min over correlated genie noises of Gaussian mutual informations at both receivers.
nodes.label: SumCapacityUpperBound

nodes.name: Proof sketch of Theorem 6
nodes.statement: We use a genie aided approach similar to \cite{AnnapureddyVeeravalli} to bound $R_1+R_2$ and $R_3$. After adding the bounds, we observe that their sum is maximized by Gaussian inputs and we obtain the upper bound. Details are given in Appendix \ref{SumCapacityUpperBoundProof}.
nodes.statement_short: Genie-aided bounds on $R_1+R_2$ and $R_3$, summed and maximized by Gaussian inputs; details in the appendix.

nodes.name: Genie-aided bounds
nodes.statement: We use a genie aided approach similar to \cite{AnnapureddyVeeravalli} to bound $R_1+R_2$ and $R_3$.
nodes.statement_short: Bound $R_1+R_2$ and $R_3$ with a genie as in Annapureddy-Veeravalli.

nodes.name: Gaussian inputs maximize the sum
nodes.statement: After adding the bounds, we observe that their sum is maximized by Gaussian inputs and we obtain the upper bound. Details are given in Appendix \ref{SumCapacityUpperBoundProof}.
nodes.statement_short: The summed bound is maximized by Gaussian inputs.

nodes.name: Treating-interference-as-noise sum capacity lower bound
nodes.statement:
A trivial sum capacity lower bound is obtained by using Gaussian codes and treating interference as noise. The resulting lower bound is given by
\begin{align} C_\Sigma\geq\underline{C}_\Sigma&=\frac{1}{2}\log\left(1+\frac{P_1+P_2}{1+h_{31}^2P_3}\right)\nonumber\\
&\quad+\frac{1}{2}\log\left(1+\frac{P_3}{1+h_{12}^2P_1+h_{22}^2P_2}\right).
\end{align}
assumptions: using Gaussian codes and treating interference as noise
nodes.statement_short: Gaussian codes with interference treated as noise give the sum-rate lower bound $\underline{C}_\Sigma$.

nodes.name: Upper bound nearly tight at low SNR
nodes.statement: In Figure \ref{Figure:SumCapacity}, we plot the upper bound $\overline{C}_\Sigma$ and the lower bound $\underline{C}_\Sigma$ as a function of SNR, the ration between the transmit power and the noise variance, for an IMAC with $P_1=P_2=P_3=P$, $h_{12}=h_{31}=0.2$, and $h_{22}=0.1$. Notice that this upper bound is nearly tight up to some value of SNR. Intuitively, this means that below some threshold value of the interference power, treating interference as noise achieves sum rate very close to the sum capacity $C_\Sigma$.
nodes.statement_short: Numerically the upper and lower sum-capacity bounds nearly coincide up to some SNR, so TIN is near-optimal at weak interference.

nodes.name: Sum capacity under symmetric weak interference
nodes.statement: In the special case of $h_{12}=h_{22}=h$, then the PIMAC becomes similar to a 2-user IC with transmit signals $X_1^n+X_2^n$ and $X_3^n$. In this case, the bounds $\overline{C}_\Sigma$ in Theorem (\ref{SumCapacityUpperBound}) and $\underline{C}_\Sigma$ in (\ref{CS_LB}) coincide if $|h|(1+h_{31}^2P_3)+|h_{31}|(1+h^2(P_1+P_2))\leq1$.
nodes.statement_short: For $h_{12}=h_{22}=h$ the PIMAC acts like a 2-user IC and the bounds coincide under a noisy-interference condition.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 1
nodes.statement_short: Trivial P2P and MAC bounds; then a genie gives $m_2$ to receiver 2, which builds a less noisy copy of $Y_1$ when $h_{12}^2\geq1$ (Sato-type argument).

nodes.name: Interference-free bounds
nodes.statement_short: Rates are bounded by the interference-free P2P capacity and MAC region.

nodes.name: Genie-aided channel
nodes.statement: Now we derive the other bounds. A genie gives $m_2$ as additional information to the second receiver. The obtained genie aided channel has a larger capacity region than the original PIMAC and can be used to outer bound $\mathcal{C}$.
nodes.statement_short: A genie gives $m_2$ to receiver 2; the enlarged channel outer bounds $\mathcal{C}$.

nodes.name: Construct a less noisy signal
nodes.statement_short: Receiver 2 decodes $m_3$ and, knowing $m_2$, builds $\tilde{Y}_1^n$.

nodes.name: Bound on $(R_1,R_3)$
nodes.statement_short: If $h_{12}^2\geq1$, $\tilde{Y}_1^n$ is less noisy, so receiver 2 decodes $m_1$ too: $(R_1,R_3)$ lies in a MAC region.

nodes.name: Bound on $(R_2,R_3)$
nodes.statement_short: Symmetric argument for $(R_2,R_3)$.

nodes.name: Bound on $(R_1,R_2,R_3)$
nodes.statement_short: If $h_{31}^2\geq1$, receiver 1 can also decode $m_3$, giving the 3-user MAC bound.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 2
nodes.statement:
We can expand the achievable region $\underline{\mathcal{C}}$
to obtain the following rate constraints for the achievable region
\begin{align*}
R_1&\leq\frac{1}{2}\log(1+\min\{P_1,h_{12}^2P_1\})\\
R_2&\leq\frac{1}{2}\log(1+\min\{P_2,h_{22}^2P_2\})\\
R_3&\leq\frac{1}{2}\log(1+\min\{P_3,h_{31}^2P_3\})\\
R_1+R_2&\leq\frac{1}{2}\log(1+\min\{P_1+P_2,h_{12}^2P_1+h_{22}^2P_2\})\\
R_1+R_3&\leq\frac{1}{2}\log(1+\min\{P_1+h_{31}^2P_3,h_{12}^2P_1+P_3\})\\
R_2+R_3&\leq\frac{1}{2}\log(1+\min\{P_2+h_{31}^2P_3,h_{22}^2P_2+P_3\})\\



R_1+R_2+R_3&\leq\frac{1}{2}\log(1+\min\{P_1+P_2+h_{31}^2P_3,\\
&\hspace{3cm}h_{12}^2P_1+h_{22}^2P_2+P_3\})
\end{align*}
Using conditions (\ref{pSI1}) and (\ref{pSI2}), these constraints reduce to
\begin{align*}
R_i&\leq\frac{1}{2}\log(1+P_i),\ \forall i\in\{1,2,3\}\\
R_1+R_2&\leq\frac{1}{2}\log(1+P_1+P_2)\\
R_1+R_3&\leq\frac{1}{2}\log(1+P_1+h_{31}^2P_3)\\
R_1+R_3&\leq\frac{1}{2}\log(1+h_{12}^2P_1+P_3)\\
R_2+R_3&\leq\frac{1}{2}\log(1+P_2+h_{31}^2P_3)\\
R_2+R_3&\leq\frac{1}{2}\log(1+h_{22}^2P_2+P_3)\\
R_1+R_2+R_3&\leq\frac{1}{2}\log(1+P_1+P_2+h_{31}^2P_3).
\end{align*}
Expanding $\overline{\mathcal{C}}$ when conditions (\ref{pSI1}) and (\ref{pSI2}) hold lead to the same rate constraints. Thus, the two regions $\overline{\mathcal{C}}$ and $\underline{\mathcal{C}}$ coincide and the result follows.
nodes.statement_short: Expand both regions into explicit rate constraints and check that under (6)-(7) they coincide.

nodes.name: Expand the inner bound
nodes.statement:
We can expand the achievable region $\underline{\mathcal{C}}$
to obtain the following rate constraints for the achievable region
\begin{align*}
R_1&\leq\frac{1}{2}\log(1+\min\{P_1,h_{12}^2P_1\})\\
R_2&\leq\frac{1}{2}\log(1+\min\{P_2,h_{22}^2P_2\})\\
R_3&\leq\frac{1}{2}\log(1+\min\{P_3,h_{31}^2P_3\})\\
R_1+R_2&\leq\frac{1}{2}\log(1+\min\{P_1+P_2,h_{12}^2P_1+h_{22}^2P_2\})\\
R_1+R_3&\leq\frac{1}{2}\log(1+\min\{P_1+h_{31}^2P_3,h_{12}^2P_1+P_3\})\\
R_2+R_3&\leq\frac{1}{2}\log(1+\min\{P_2+h_{31}^2P_3,h_{22}^2P_2+P_3\})\\



R_1+R_2+R_3&\leq\frac{1}{2}\log(1+\min\{P_1+P_2+h_{31}^2P_3,\\
&\hspace{3cm}h_{12}^2P_1+h_{22}^2P_2+P_3\})
\end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Write $\underline{\mathcal{C}}$ as explicit min-type rate constraints.

nodes.name: Reduce under the conditions
nodes.statement:
Using conditions (\ref{pSI1}) and (\ref{pSI2}), these constraints reduce to
\begin{align*}
R_i&\leq\frac{1}{2}\log(1+P_i),\ \forall i\in\{1,2,3\}\\
R_1+R_2&\leq\frac{1}{2}\log(1+P_1+P_2)\\
R_1+R_3&\leq\frac{1}{2}\log(1+P_1+h_{31}^2P_3)\\
R_1+R_3&\leq\frac{1}{2}\log(1+h_{12}^2P_1+P_3)\\
R_2+R_3&\leq\frac{1}{2}\log(1+P_2+h_{31}^2P_3)\\
R_2+R_3&\leq\frac{1}{2}\log(1+h_{22}^2P_2+P_3)\\
R_1+R_2+R_3&\leq\frac{1}{2}\log(1+P_1+P_2+h_{31}^2P_3).
\end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Conditions (6)-(7) resolve each minimum.

nodes.name: Compare with the outer bound
nodes.statement: Expanding $\overline{\mathcal{C}}$ when conditions (\ref{pSI1}) and (\ref{pSI2}) hold lead to the same rate constraints. Thus, the two regions $\overline{\mathcal{C}}$ and $\underline{\mathcal{C}}$ coincide and the result follows.
nodes.statement_short: The outer bound yields the same constraints, so the regions coincide.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 6
nodes.statement_short: Genie-aided bound with correlated side information, Fano and chain rule. The key step shows Gaussian inputs maximize the bound via Annapureddy-Veeravalli's Lemma 6 and the worst-case noise result.

nodes.name: Genie side information
nodes.statement_short: Define genie signals $S_i^n$ with noise correlated to $Z_i$ and give them to the receivers.

nodes.name: Fano's inequality
nodes.statement_short: Fano bounds $R_1+R_2$ and $R_3$ by mutual informations with side information.

nodes.name: Chain rule
nodes.statement_short: Expand both bounds into differential entropies (Q1), (Q2).

nodes.name: Goal: Gaussian inputs are optimal
nodes.statement: The next step is to show that sum of the above quantities (\ref{Q1}) and (\ref{Q2}) are maximized when $X_i^n$ is i.i.d. Gaussian for all $i\in\{1,2,3\}$, i.e. $X_i\sim\mathcal{N}(0,P_i^*)$ where $P_i^*\leq P_i$. We will denote that Gaussian $X_i$ as $X_{iG}$ and the corresponding outputs as $Y_{iG}$ and $S_{iG}$.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to showing i.i.d. Gaussian inputs maximize the sum.

nodes.name: Conditional entropy terms
nodes.statement_short: Gaussian maximizes conditional entropy under covariance constraint.

nodes.name: Joint maximization of the difference
nodes.statement:
Furthermore, the terms $h(S_1^n|X_1^n,X_2^n)$ and $h(S_2^n|X_3^n)$ are independent of the distribution of $X_i$. Now, we jointly maximize the difference $h(S_1^n)-h(Y_2^n|S_2^n,X_3^n)$ as follows
\begin{align}
&\hspace{-1cm}h(S_1^n)-h(Y_2^n|S_2^n,X_3^n)\nonumber\\
&=h(h_{12}X_1^n+h_{22}X_2^n+\eta_1W_1^n)\nonumber\\
&\quad-h(h_{12}X_1^n+h_{22}X_2^n+Z_2^n|W_2^n)\\
&\stackrel{(a)}{=}h(h_{12}X_1^n+h_{22}X_2^n+\eta_1W_1^n)\nonumber\\
&\quad-h(h_{12}X_1^n+h_{22}X_2^n+V_2^n)\\
&\stackrel{(b)}{\leq}nh(h_{12}X_{1G}+h_{22}X_{2G}+\eta_1W_1)\nonumber\\
&\quad-nh(h_{12}X_{1G}+h_{22}X_{2G}+V_2)\\ &=nh(S_{1G})-nh(Y_{2G}|S_{2G},X_{3G},X_{4G}),
\end{align}
where $(a)$ follows from \cite[Lemma 6]{AnnapureddyVeeravalli} with $V_2^n$ being an i.i.d. Gaussian sequence with $V_2\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1-\rho_2^2)$ and $(b)$ from the worst case noise \cite{DiggaviCover} such that $\eta_1^2\leq 1-\rho_2^2$.
nodes.statement_short: Bound $h(S_1^n)-h(Y_2^n|S_2^n,X_3^n)$ by its Gaussian value using AV Lemma 6 and worst-case noise.

nodes.name: Monotonicity in powers
nodes.statement: Since $\eta_1^2\leq1-\rho_2^2$, (\ref{T1}) can be shown to be increasing in $P_1^*$ and $P_2^*$ and thus is maximized by $X_{iG}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,P_i)$. Similarly, if $\eta_2^2\leq1-\rho_1^2$, $h(S_2^n)-h(Y_1^n|S_1^n,X_1^n,X_2^n)$ can be shown to be maximized by $X_{iG}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,P_i)$. Moreover, $h(Y_{1G}|S_{1G})$ and $h(Y_{2G}|S_{2G})$ can be shown to be increasing in $P_i^*$ and thus also maximized by $X_{iG}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,P_i)$.
nodes.statement_short: All terms increase in the input powers, so full power Gaussian inputs are optimal.

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement:
As a result, by letting $n\to\infty$
\begin{align} &R_1+R_2+R_3\nonumber\\
&\quad\leq I(X_{1G},X_{2G};Y_{1G},S_{1G})+I(X_{3G};Y_{2G},S_{2G})
\end{align}
with $X_{iG}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,P_i)$ and $\eta_i\leq1-\rho_j^2$.
nodes.statement_short: Letting $n\to\infty$ yields the sum-rate upper bound.
